Thus, affected the fair presentation of the FS.
observations.description:
1.1. Section 74 of PD No. 1445

Monthly reports of depositories to agency head. At the close of each month, depositories shall report to the agency head, in such form as he may direct, the condition of the agency account standing on their books. The head of the agency shall see to it that a reconciliation is made between the balance shown in the reports and the balance found in the books of the agency.

1.5. The discrepancies are due to unrecorded disbursements/deposits, debit memo, debit advice and stale checks, and uncorrected book errors from CYs 2019 to 2023. Of the P182,122,739.06 unadjusted book reconciling items, a total of P170,470,782.38 or 93.60 percent are attributable to unrecorded disbursements and deposits. The position of the Office of the City Accountant (OCAT) on the significant amounts from the two reconciling items are the following:

Unrecorded disbursements – these are approved disbursement vouchers that were already forwarded by the OCAT to the City Treasurer’s Office (CTO) for check preparation and payment. The CTO had already prepared and issued the check and the amounts were already reflected in the bank statements. However, the supporting documents, including the copies of checks issued were not returned to the OCAT for recording which resulted to overstatement of the applicable CiB account and other affected accounts in the FS; and

Unrecorded deposits – are collections mostly obtained from unknown third-party deposits. The income to be recognized or the liability to be derecognized in connection with the deposits remain undetermined. Thus, understated cash in bank, the related income, and/or overstated the associated liability account.

1.6. The fundamental purpose of the preparation of the BRS is to evaluate recorded balances against that of bank accounts and to determine causes of variances, if any. The OCAT should draw journal entry vouchers to record all valid reconciling items that require correction in the books. However, the retention of records in the CTO after the preparation and issuance of checks, and the absence of a timely reconciliation between the two offices hindered the prompt recording of reconciling items. Hence, the faithful representation of transactions affecting the cash in bank accounts was not attained which affected the fair presentation of FS.

observations.title: The accuracy, completeness, and reliability of the year-end balance of Accounts Payable (AP) amounting to P4.577 billion could not be determined due to net understatement variance of P525.085 million from confirmation results with contractors/suppliers as against balances per books contrary to Paragraph 27 of International Public Sector Accounting Standard (IPSAS) 1. Thus, affecting the fair presentation of the FS.
observations.description:
2.1. We audited the City’s Accounts Payable to ascertain if carrying amounts presented in the FS as of December 31, 2023: (a) exist and are indeed firm liabilities; (b) complete and accurately valued; (c) have been accounted for in accordance with pertinent laws, rules and regulations and the IPSAS.

2.2. Our procedures include, among others, (i) vouching against procurement and disbursement documents; (ii) examination of procurement documents; (iii) cut-off test and other test of details, balances and disclosures; (iv) confirmation; and (v) account analysis.

2.3. Section 10, Chapter 1, of the MNGAS for LGUs, Volume II, prescribes the use of a SL. The SL is a book of final entry containing the details or breakdown of the balances of the controlling account appearing in the General Ledger (GL). Postings to the SLs generally come from source documents. The totals of the SL balances shall be reconciled with their respective control account in the GL at the end of every month.

2.4. Verification of the Statement of Financial Position as of December 31, 2023, and its GLs and SLs, under all funds, shows that the AP had an outstanding balance of P4,577,292,672.32. Details are as follows:

Table 6- Comparative CYs 2023 and 2022 Payables

| Fund | 2023 | 2022 | Inc. (Dec.) | % Change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GF | P3,402,911,945.76 | P4,724,971,723.56 | (P1,322,059,777.80) | -28% |
| SEF | 1,152,098,415.86 | 324,350,345.48 | 827,748,070.38 | 255% |
| TF | 22,282,310.7 | 29,092,419.59 | (6,810,108.89) | -23% |
| Total | P4,577,292,672.32 | P5,078,414,488.63 | (P501,121,816.31) | -10% |

2.5. Confirmation letters (CLs) were sent by the Audit Team to 24 contractors/suppliers to verify their respective claims/receivables against the City’s financial records. The book balance of the AP subjected for confirmation amounted to P1,518,577,125.73 or equivalent to 33.18 percent of the total AP balance.

2.6. As of writing, out of the 24 CLs, eight replies or 33 percent had been received for payables totaling P766,770,889.59 as against its book balance of P241,684,969.43. The results of the confirmation disclosed a net understatement of P525,085,920.16. Details are presented in Table 7:

Table 7- Comparison of Accounts Payable per books and per confirmation

| Contractor/ Supplier | Per Books | Per CL | Over (Under) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Supplier No. 1 | P40,874,177.52 | P 92,108,963.25 | (P51,234,785.73) |
| Supplier No. 2 | 15,955,008.14 | 25,458,066.52 | (9,503,058.38) |
| Supplier No. 3 | 30,421,764.36 | 286,009,237.91 | (255,587,473.55) |
| Supplier No. 4 | 43,126,979.89 | 37,283,099.99 | 5,843,879.90 |
| Supplier No. 5 | 2,080,028.58 | 82,386,012.65 | (80,305,984.07) |
| Supplier No. 6 | 14,870,005.88 | 15,861,339.61 | (991,333.73) |
| Supplier No. 7 | 15,586,319.10 | 127,424,305.29 | (111,837,986.19) |
| Supplier No. 8 | 78,770,685.96 | 100,239,864.37 | (21,469,178.41) |
| Total | P241,684,969.43 | P766,770,889.59 | (P525,085,920.16) |

2.7. Considering that only 33.18 percent of the total AP balance had undergone confirmation and only 33 percent thereof replied, it may be presumed the net variance of P525,085,920.16 will substantially change as the sample size is increased.

2.8. Moreover, it was observed that the OCAT did not maintain a separate SL for each of the contractors/suppliers but instead only SLs grouped generally as to the class of expenditure such as Maintenance and Other Operating Expenses (MOOE) and Capital Outlay (CO). The ledger should reflect the recognition of payables to a contractor/supplier as well as payments/settlements made thereafter and the outstanding balance. The absence of individual/separate SL balances resulted in unmonitored outstanding payable balances for each creditor at any given time which is contrary to Paragraph 27 of IPSAS 1.

recommendations.text: Maintain a separate SL for each contractor/supplier for proper monitoring of each outstanding payable and status of accounts.

observations.title: Insufficient imposition of Real Property Tax (RPT) and Special Education Tax (SET) by the City due to: a) Misplaced application of the Assessment Levels (ALs) prescribed under Section 12 of Ordinance No. 8331, s. 2013; and b) Omission of 1,130 Real Property Units (RPUs) in the Assessment Rolls (AR) contrary to Section 2, Chapter II, Manual on Real Property Appraisal and Assessment Operations (MRPAAO), thereby diminishing the City’s earnings to be utilized to finance its programs/projects/activities (PPAs).
observations.description:
3.1. The Assessed Values (AVs) of 452 RPUs were understated due to the misplaced application of Assessment Levels (ALs) prescribed under Section 12 of Ordinance No. 8331, s. 2013 resulting in insufficient imposition of RPT and SET by P2,182,761.77 and P1,153,777.74, respectively, for a total of P3,336,539.51 in CY 2023.

3.2. Section 12 of Ordinance No. 8331, s. 2013, states that:

A.) The assessment levels to be applied to the fair market value of real property to determine its assessed value shall be as follows:

1.) On lands:

|  | P 300,000.00 | 30% |

| 1,000,000.00 | 2,000,000.00 | 60% |
| 2,000,000.00 | 5,000,000.00 | 70% |
| 5,000,000.00 | 10,000,000.00 | 75% |
| 10,000,000.00 |  | 80% |

3.3. The prescribed ALs under Section 12 of the above-mentioned Ordinance are compliant with Section 218 of RA No. 7160, otherwise known as, “The Local Government Code of 1991.” Said ALs were already adopted by the City Assessor’s Office starting CY 2014 in the computation of AVs or the Taxable Value, which was the basis in the calculation of the Real Property and Special Education Taxes by the City Treasurer’s Office.

3.4. The City Government uses the Real Property Tax Assessment System (RPTAS) to facilitate the recording and reporting of Market Values and AVs of real properties and billing and collection of real property taxes within the jurisdiction of the City. The System includes Assessment, Billing and Collection Modules. The data provided by the Assessment module such as the AVs of real properties are automatically linked to the Billing and Collection Modules. The AVs are the reference for the computation and imposition of RPT and SET by the City Treasurer’s Office.

3.5. The City Assessor’s Office submitted an Assessment Roll (AR) for taxable real properties which registered 409,652 RPUs with effectivity of assessment as of CY 2023. The following information prescribed by the Manual on Real Property Appraisal and Assessment Operations (2006 Edition) are met:

a. Property Identification Number that includes coding system for the City, District, Barangay and Section;

b. Property Owner;

c. Address of the Property Owner;

d. Kind and Classification of the Property;

e. Fair Market Value of the Property;

f. Assessment Level;

g. Assessed Value of the Property;

h. Previous and Current ARPN; and

i. Effectivity of Assessment

a) Misplaced application of the ALs

3.6. We tested the accuracy of the computation of the ALs and determine if they have been correctly assessed in accordance with the rates provided in aforesaid Section of the Ordinance. Review of the computation disclosed that the ALs applied to 452 RPUs were lower than the rates provided therein. As a result, the AVs of these RPUs were understated, thus, the RPT and SET were under imposed by P2,182,761.77 and P1,153,777.74, respectively, for a total of P3,336,539.51 in CY 2023 as shown in Table 8.

Table 8. Difference between RPT and SET per Certified List and Per Audit of 452 RPUs

| Particulars | RPT | SET | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per Certified List of Taxpayers | 4,405,552.24 | 2,567,087.11 | 6,972,639.35 |
| Per Audit | 6,588,314.01 | 3,720,864.85 | 10,309,178.86 |
| Underassessment | (2,182,761.77) | (1,153,777.74) | (3,336,539.51) |

3.7. Since the City uses the RPTAS, it is expected that the System process the data accurately, the programs embedded therein verifies and controls the data before and during processing. However, the foregoing deficiencies indicate that the System lacks the controls to check/detect inaccurate calculations in ALs.

b) Omission of 1,130 RPUs in the AR

3.8. 1,130 RPUs that were drawn from the 474 sampled tax maps were not in the AR as of CY 2023, contrary to the objectives on establishing a complete inventory of all real properties and providing a permanent link between real properties and office records as mentioned in Section 2, Chapter II, MRPAAO. Consequently, these RPUs were not included for imposition of realty taxes thus, depriving the City to earn its rightful income to finance its PPAs.

3.9. Section 2, Chapter II, MRPAAO:

SECTION 2. – Tax Mapping Operations

Tax maps are the single most important tool in the real property assessment process. It is not possible to establish an adequate real property tax record and accounting system without tax maps, for they are the basic foundation of the system. They establish a permanent link between the real properties in the field and the property assessment and tax records in the office. They are indispensable in the discovery of property and the identification of property ownership. They simplify the task of property description and tie together all property records, including field appraisal and assessment sheets and assessment and tax rolls. They also provide the public with vital real property information. Finally, tax maps make possible the establishment of a property record system that is easily adapted to data computerization.

A. Objectives of the Tax Mapping Operations

1. To establish a complete inventory of all real properties;

2. To provide a permanent link between real properties and office records;

3. To identify the ownership of every piece of real property; and

4. To account for the total land area of provinces, cities or municipalities.

3.10. Based on the above definition and provision, the tax map is a graphical presentation of all real properties. It serves as the link between the real properties and the office records such as the Assessment Roll, and aids in identifying real properties that are taxable or not. It assigns a unique numbering system in order to account all real properties actually existing in the field and it helps in determining undiscovered properties for taxation purposes.

3.11. The Tax Mapping Division of the City Assessor’s Office is responsible for the maintenance of tax maps and for the preservation of the integrity of the identification numbering system. Tax map maintenance is defined as the technical revision of the tax map document, as differentiated from the care and storage of tax maps. Any one or all of the following assessment record forms may be affected by changes in ownership, value, or land area:

i. Tax Map including Tax Map Control Roll

ii. Property Identification Number (PIN)

iii. Tax Declaration

iv. Assessment Roll

v. Real Property Field Appraisal and Assessment Sheet

vi. Property Ownership Card

vii. Tax Collection Record

3.12. The Tax Mapping Division is responsible for recording changes in the first two (2) assessment record forms mentioned above. Changes affecting the other official records are the responsibility of other divisions. Revision of tax maps and the property identification numbering system occur as the result of changes in land area only.

3.13. We sampled 474 tax maps of real properties in the City and observed that there are 1,130 PINs or RPUs for the Land in the tax maps which were not included in the AR, as summarized in Table 9. This is an indication that not all real properties found in the field, drawn thru graphical presentation and inscribed in the tax map were appraised and assessed for taxation purposes.

Table 9. RPUs in the Tax Maps sample but not in the AR as of CY 2023

| District | No. of Maps Sampled | No. of RPUs in the Maps | No. of RPUs in the Maps but not in the AR as of CY 2023 |

| Sta. Cruz | 46 | 1,587 | 83 |
| Sampaloc | 51 | 1,340 | 89 |
| San Miguel | 31 | 518 | 111 |
| Malate | 74 | 2,825 | 226 |
| Ermita | 19 | 556 | 47 |
| Sta. Ana | 13 | 486 | 50 |
| Paco | 10 | 691 | 243 |
| Pandacan | 135 | 627 | 140 |
| Total | 474 | 10,990 | 1,130 |

3.14. Consequently, these RPUs were not included for imposition of realty taxes. Thus, deprived the City of its rightful income to finance its PPAs.

3.15. Moreover, the objectives of tax mapping operations particularly on establishing a complete inventory of all real properties and providing a permanent link between real properties and office records such as the assessment roll mentioned in Section 2, Chapter II, MRPAAO, were not fully achieved.

observations.management_comment:
3.17. The Department of Assessment (DOA) was able to identify 1,613 RPUs (441 land, 1008 improvement, 164 machinery), out of which 380 RPUs were corrected. Tax mapping division is presently reviewing the 1,130 PINs or RPUs.

3.18. Some of these RPUs were verified to be mother PINs which were already cancelled due to segregation of the land property. A traceback of available records is presently being conducted to identify whether these RPUs were omitted during the preparation of the General Revision 2014.

3.19. The CTO shall collect the RPT due that correspond to the erroneous application of assessment level by the DOA once adjustments are made on the assessment level and assessed values.

observations.title: Out of 222 Gender and Development (GAD) PPAs, 22 were unimplemented and 84 were not reported in the GAD Accomplishment Report (AR) or have no status contrary to RA No. 9710. Thus, the City’s objective of ensuring awareness and sustaining support for gender and development, women’s empowerment and response to gender issues were not fully realized.
observations.description:
4.1. We audited GAD programs implemented by the City in CY 2023 with an objective to determine compliance with the RA No. 9710 and Philippine Commission on Women (PCW), Department of Interior and Local Government (DILG), Department of Budget and Management (DBM) and National Economic Development Authority (NEDA) Joint Memorandum Circular (JMC) No. 2013-01. Our audit procedures include, among others, review of the budget and accomplishment report, examination of documents, inquiry and validation of transactions on PPAs deliveries.

4.2. Item C.8 of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA JMC No. 2013-01 dated July 18, 2013, or the Guidelines on the Localization of the Magna Carta of Women, provides the guidelines on the preparation and submission of LGU GAD Accomplishment Reports (AR), such as:

(1) The GAD Focal Point System (GFPS) shall prepare their annual GAD AR based on the DILG-approved GPB or the enacted GPB following the form prescribed in Annex E. Activities completed until the end of the year may be included in the final LGU GAD AR.

4.3. Section 4.1.C.7.4 of the same JMC also provides that the GFPS shall regularly monitor if the GAD budget is utilized for its intended purpose and to verify the actual cost of implementing GAD activities.

4.4. Further, Section 6.1 of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA Joint Circular No. 2016-01 amending Section 4.1.C.7.1 of PCW-DILG-DBM-NEDA Joint Circular No. 2013-01 states that the Local Chief Executive (LCE) shall issue an appropriate policy directive, copy furnished the DILG Office that conducted the review of the LGU GAD Plan and Budget (GPB), to disseminate and implement GPB.

4.5. Review of the GPB for CY 2023 submitted to the Office of the City Auditor showed that the City is compliant under the Magna Carta of Women, wherein the GAD Fund shall be at least five percent (5%) of the agency’s total budget appropriations. The City allocated P1,355,026,860.09 for GAD fund, or 6.10 percent of the total appropriation of P22.200 billion for CY 2023. Details are presented in Table 10:

4.6. Validation of the GAD AR submitted on 23 February 2024 showed that of the 222 planned PPAs listed in the CY 2023 GPB, 116 PPAs with a budget of P1,264,923,263.00 or 52.25 percent of the total planned PPAs were implemented during the year, 22 PPAs with a budget of P37,503,967.59 were not implemented during the year, while 84 PPAs listed in the GPB with a total budget of P52,599,629.50 were not among those PPAs listed in the GAD AR. Hence, no status or update on the implementation of the said PPAs. As summarized in Table 11.

4.7. Based on the GAD AR and verification with the GAD Focal Person, a catch-up plan will be implemented for some of the unimplemented PPAs during the year. Other PPAs are still in the planning or development phase. Meanwhile, the 84 PPAs with no status or update on its implementation, are yet to be verified.

4.8. Review of the GAD AR also showed 44 implemented GAD PPAs but were not among those included in the GPB for CY 2023.

4.9. Also noteworthy is that implemented PPAs in CY 2023 decreased to 52.25 percent (116 out of 222 PPAs) as compared to the 76.06 percent implementation rate (143 out of 188 PPAs) in CY 2022, although there was an increase in the number of PPAs listed in the GPB. Details are as follows:

4.11. Due to the non-implementation of other GAD PPAs, the City’s objective to support gender and development, women’s empowerment and responding to gender issues were not fully attained as planned. Further, the under-utilization of the GAD Fund merits a Management review on how to better address the gaps that adversely affected the full implementation of PPAs.

observations.title: A total of P472.416 million withheld for CY 2023 remittances to the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR), Government Service Insurance System (GSIS), Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth have not been remitted by the City contrary to existing rules and regulations.
observations.section_heading: COMPLIANCE WITH TAX LAWS AND OTHER REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS
observations.description:
5.1. We audited Inter-Agency Payables to determine whether 1) the amounts being withheld by City are promptly remitted to appropriate agencies and 2) the unremitted balances are correctly reported in the FS.

5.2. Our audit of these accounts is guided by the following provisions:

BIR

5.3. Section 4.1 of Revenue Regulations No. 6-2006 dated July 31, 2001:

RETURNS AND PAYMENT OF TAXES WITHHELD AT SOURCE. When to File- For both large and non-large taxpayers, the withholding tax return, whether creditable or final (including final withholding taxes on interest from any currency bank deposit and yield or any other monetary benefit from deposit substitutes and from trust funds and similar arrangements) shall be filed and payments should be made, within ten (10) days after the end of each month, except for taxes withheld for the month of December of each year, which shall be filed on or before January 15 of the following year.

FILING OF RETURN AND PAYMENT OF INCOME TAX WITHHELD ON COMPENSATION (FORM NO. 1601). - Every person required to deduct and withhold the tax on compensation, including large taxpayers as determined by the Commissioner, shall make a return and pay such tax on or before the 10th day of the month following the month in which withholding was made to any authorized agent bank within the Revenue District Office (RDO) or in places where there are no agent banks, to the Revenue District Officer of the City or Municipality where the withholding agent/employer’s legal residence or place of business or office is located; xxx (Emphasis supplied)

GSIS

5.4. Section 6 (B) of Republic Act No. 8291 provides that each employer shall remit directly to the GSIS the employees’ and employers’ contributions within the first ten (10) days of the calendar month following the month to which the contributions apply. The remittance by the employer of the contributions to the GSIS shall take priority over and above the payment of any and all obligations, except salaries and wages of its employees.

Pag-IBIG

5.5. Section 3(a) and (b) Rule VII of the Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR) of RA No. 9679 or the Home Development Mutual Fund (HDMF) Law of 2009 provides that all employers shall remit to the Fund their contributions and the contributions of their covered employees as well as the latter’s loan amortizations or payments to the Fund, as provided for under Section 2 of this Rule, when applicable, within fifteen (15) days from the date the same were collected unless another period is previously agreed upon between the employer and the Fund, or within such periods as the Fund may prescribe otherwise. xxx

5.6. Every employer required to set aside and remit such contributions as prescribed under R.A. No. 9679 and these Rules shall be liable for their payment, and non-payment thereof shall further subject the employer to a penalty of three percent (3%) per month of the amounts payable from the date the contributions fall due until paid.

5.7. Every employer who actually deducts from the salary of his employee the latter’s loan amortization or payments to the Fund, as provided for under these Rules, shall be liable for their payment, and non-payment thereof shall likewise further subject the employer to a penalty of three percent (3%) per month of the amounts payable from the date the loan amortizations or payments fall due until paid.

PhilHealth

5.8. Section 19(b) of the revised IRR of the National Health Insurance Act of 2013 provides that the monthly premium contribution of employed members shall be remitted by the employer on or before the tenth (10th) calendar day of the month following the applicable month for which the payment is due and applicable.

5.9. Analysis of the Inter-agency payables accounts disclosed that amounts withheld during CY 2023 totaling P472,416,074.60 (Table 14) were not remitted, contrary to afore-mentioned provisions.

Table 14: Inter-Agency Payables Schedule

|  | BIR | GSIS | Pag-IBIG | PhilHealth | Total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Beginning Balance | P427,193,827.17 | P67,921,778.67 | P17,054,734.75 | P36,922,498.51 | P 549,092,839.10 |
| Add: Accrual (CY 2023) | 852,938,415.46 | 1,292,196,017.21 | 65,762,890.00 | 129,203,097.92 | 2,340,100,420.59 |
| Total | 1,280,132,242.63 | 1,360,117,795.88 | 82,817,624.75 | 166,125,596.43 | 2,889,193,259.69 |
| Less: Remittance (CY 2023) | 807,279,774.81 | 1,234,478,581.61 | 54,959,608.14 | 132,420,490.86 | 2,229,137,455.42 |
| Ending Balance (CY 2023) | 472,852,467.82 | 125,639,214.27 | 27,858,016.61 | 33,705,105.57 | 660,055,804.27 |
| Less: Remittance (January CY 2024) | 91,338,777.20 | 90,083,303.52 | 5,937,515.95 | 280,133.00 | 187,639,729.67 |
| Unremitted Balance | P381,513,690.62 | P35,555,910.75 | P21,921,500.66 | P33,424,972.57 | P472,416,074.60 |

5.10. This non-remittance to BIR, GSIS, Pag-IBIG, and PhilHealth may result in the imposition of avoidable interests, penalties and surcharges, not to mention the possibility of denial of employee benefits due to insufficient mandatory remittances.

recommendations.text: We recommended and Management agreed to ensure prompt and full remittance of all withholding taxes, contributions, premium payments, loan amortization and other amounts due to the BIR, GSIS, Pag-IBIG and PhilHealth pursuant to the above-mentioned regulations.

observations.management_comment:
5.12. The Management commented that the Due to BIR unremitted amounts pertain to tax withheld in connection with the unpaid accounts payable as of year-end of the City. These amounts will be remitted the following year once said accounts payable is paid subject to the availability of cash being as the normal practice of the City’s cash management.

5.13. As for the Due to the GSIS, the remaining amount pertain to remittances withheld for clarification from various offices/departments/bureaus. These remittances are either due to newly hired or newly promoted employees, including those employees with incomplete information determined by this office which are already communicated to concerned offices/departments/bureaus. These amounts will be remitted once the respective Agency Authorized Officers of these offices/departments/bureaus have already updated the GSIS records through Agency Remittance Advice.

5.14. Due to PAG-IBIG and Due to PhilHealth represent the amount withheld as of year-end. The OCAT is in the process of reconciliation and recording of unrecorded disbursement vouchers which are not yet at the possession of this Office.

observations.title: The City was unable to identify and appropriate various PPAs for Local Climate Change Action Plan (LCCAP) in CY 2023, which is not inconsonance with Section 14 of RA No. 9729, otherwise known as the Climate Change Act of 2009, as amended.
observations.section_heading: COMPLIANCE WITH TAX LAWS AND OTHER REGULATORY REQUIREMENTS
observations.description:
6.1. Sec. 14 of RA No. 9729 provides, among others, that LGUs shall be the frontline agencies in the formulation, planning and implementation of climate change action plans in their respective areas, consistent with the provisions of the Local Government Code, the Framework, and the National Climate Change Action Plan. It further mandates that city governments shall consider climate change adaptation, as one of their regular functions. Notably, the same provision expressly authorized LGUs to appropriate and use such amount from its Internal Revenue Allotment or IRA (now National Tax Allocation or NTA) necessary to implement said local plan effectively, any provision in the Local Government Code to the contrary notwithstanding.

6.2. The audit included the determination of the City’s compliance with the requirements with the aforesaid law, as amended by RA No. 10174 and other existing rules and regulations. Specifically, to assess and validate the LCCAP Formulation Process as follows:

1. Preparatory Stage – organization of the LCCAP Core Team and orientation of LGU officials, key stakeholders, etc., on the purpose and scope of climate change adaptation planning, consultations, etc;

2. Data gathering, assessment, risk analysis and validation

3. Planning, prioritization and budgeting; and

4. Implementation, monitoring and evaluation

6.3. Records disclosed that the City Council of Manila, in its Resolution No. 214, s. 2021, dated October 4, 2021, adopted the approval of the City’s initial LCCAP for 2022-2032 which was prepared and submitted by the Manila Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO). The Philippine Climate Change Commission, in its letter dated May 4, 2022, certified its receipt of a copy of said plan as mandated by DILG MC No. 2021-068, dated June 28, 2021.

6.4. A reading of the LCCAP shows that it provides two main areas with corresponding sectors and strategies wherein possible priority programs, projects, activities and strategies may be identified for implementation, to wit:

| Area |  |
| --- | --- |
| Climate Change Mitigation | Sectors: |
|  | Energy |
|  | Transportation and Traffic Management |
|  | Agricultural |
|  | Forest and other Land Use |
|  | Industrial Processes and Product Use |
|  | Waste Management |
|  | Environment (Forestry and Other Environment Sector) |
|  | Industrial and Commercial Establishments |
|  | Science and Technology |
| Climate Change Adaptation | Strategies: |
|  | Promotion of renewable energy sources (solar, wind, etc.) |
|  | Rooftop water harvesting is to be made mandatory |
|  | Sewage system, water sanitation and wastewater treatment |
|  | Improvement of drainage system and waterways |
|  | Contraction of sea walls/breakwater |
|  | Development, installation and establishment Early Warning System |
|  | Improvement of Traffic Management |
|  | Monitoring compliance of commercial establishments in implementing strict parking regulations |
|  | Improvement and continuation of food security program |

6.5. A review of the City’s CY 2023 Annual Investment Plan (AIP) prepared by the City Planning and Development Office (CPDO) showed that it did not specifically have a list of proposed climate change PPAs for implementation during the same year. Concerned CPDO personnel explained that some PPAs may be identified and classified as climate change PPAs from among the several PPAs submitted by various City offices/departments. Concerned personnel from both the CPDO and MDRRMO however, cannot assure the specific area or strategy the purported PPAs from the AIP may refer to in the City’s LCCAP since there were no prior discussions undertaken thereon.

6.6. Notably, funds for the various PPAs submitted by different City offices/departments were to be charged from their respective approved appropriations. According to the aforementioned provision, it was categorically provided that climate change PPAs are to be funded from the City’s IRA (now NTA).

6.7. It was also admitted by said personnel that there were no submitted monitoring, assessment or evaluation reports pertaining to any climate change PPAs that could have been implemented. These reports are necessary to validate the City’s implementation of PPAs as mandated by law.

6.8. Moreover, the City was unable to create its LCCAP Core Team which is not in consonance with Paragraph 3.1.1 of Memorandum Circular (MC) No. 2014-135 dated October 21, 2014, of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).

6.9. Paragraph 3.1.1 of the MC No. 2014-135 provides that the Local Chief Executive, shall organize a LCCAP Core Team (LCT), who will lead, oversee and ensure that an LCCAP will be drafted, eventually approved, implemented, regularly monitored and updated when necessary. It recommended the following LGU offices be represented in the team: Planning and Development, Health, Engineering, Agriculture, Social Welfare and Development, Budget, Treasurer, DRRM and Local Government Operations Officer. Under Section 7 of the City’s LCCAP, it provides for the creation, my means of an Executive Order (EO), of the Climate Change Action Committee (CCAC), also called the Climate Core Team, composed of various Department Heads of the City as members with the City Mayor and City Vice Mayor as Chairman and Vice Chairman, respectively. Among the duties and responsibilities of the said CCAC is to prepare the LCCAP and facilitate effective integration of planned initiatives into the City’s development plans.

6.10. Verification revealed that the approved LCCAP was not initiated by the City’s LCT nor by the said CCAC (Climate Core Team) but was prepared and submitted to the City Council by personnel of the MDRRMO, as Main Author, Co-Authors and Chief Editors. Further inquiry disclosed that Section 7 is, to date, not implemented since a copy of the relevant EO has not been presented.

recommendations.label: a.
recommendations.text: Promptly create the City’s LCCAP Core Team in accordance with Paragraph 3.1.1 of DILG-MC No. 2014-135 and Section 7 of the City’s LCCAP to facilitate the proper planning, prioritization, funding, implementation and monitoring/assessment of proposed climate change PPAs; and
recommendations.lead_in: We recommended and Management agreed to:

recommendations.label: b.
recommendations.text: Ensure that approved climate change PPAs are aligned with the City’s LCCAP and funded from the City’s IRA (now NTA) in accordance with Section 14 of RA No. 9729.
